name: Olga Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead wheel-loader shifts at a large mine. I check the truck queue, the bucket and the turning area before the first load, then keep the drivers moving without crowding the road. My two-year technical diploma helped me into the cab, but years of difficult shifts made me the person others ask about a jam. I like teaching a safe approach and dislike a plan made from an empty yard.

say: I accept a **shorter report** while operators still watch the truck queue.
I rely on **paper counts** when radio traffic gets confused.
think: I feel **work secure** if only forms change and loader shifts remain.
I have **three months** saved while the pension still needs checking.
do: **Lead** wheel-loader shifts and count every truck load on paper before reconciling with dispatch.
**Transfer** our usual amount from each mine payday into savings while the regular bills stay covered.
feel: **Calm** about mild AI change and steady household pay.
S0.quote: My partner would ask whether the same number of shifts is paid and whether the pension statement arrived.
fieldNote: **Experienced loading** and steady wages make limited AI a manageable change.
**Three-month cushion** supports calm, though pension figures remain a task.
**No AI use** fits her resistant profile; she keeps a practical paper count.

steps.text: Keep leading wheel-loader shifts and counting trucks on paper
Transfer the usual payday amount into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the loading crew that a shorter report is welcome, but somebody still has to watch the truck line and the bucket. I have never used AI, and my handwritten queue notes have kept the trucks moving for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be comfortable if change stayed that small. My partner and I have around three months of costs saved, my pay is regular, and our children support themselves now. We still need to check the pension, but we can do that without a technology scare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the wheel-loader shifts and check the truck count on paper. In the first year I would put our usual amount into savings each payday and compare the monthly roster with actual paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The mine has changed its forms before and we carried on loading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the paper count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A line of trucks can change during a radio fault, and I can mark each load while I am in the cab. I reconcile the sheet with dispatch after the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether the same number of shifts is paid and whether the pension statement arrived. Those are better questions for us than whether a form looks modern.

say: I expect **truck plans** to change before loading work does.
I want a **full-shift trial** before software affects crew numbers.
think: I worry **planners** may lose work first.
I expect my **own shifts** to continue now, with later robots worth watching.
do: **Record** missed loads and blocked turns against dispatch plans.
**Wait** for trial results before accepting a new crew pattern.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues and future crew cuts, while loading shifts look sound now.
S1.quote: I will judge a machine after it works a whole shift.
fieldNote: **Full-shift evidence** is her standard because real queues and delays reveal failures.
**Slow screen adoption** is acknowledged without promising a new AI skill.
**Own work** appears secure near term; office planners feel the first change.

steps.text: Keep the current wheel-loader rota while dispatch changes
Wait for full-shift trial results before accepting a new crew pattern

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software may plan truck arrivals, but a loader operator must still see when a queue blocks the turning area. I would ask dispatch to test the new plan with a full shift, not an empty yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planners could lose tasks first, and I would not like seeing someone pushed out by a screen. Robots move into loading more slowly, so I expect my own shifts to continue for now. I still want to see any crew proposal in writing before the mine buys machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current loading rota and compare the new dispatch plan with truck queues. In the first year I would write down missed loads and ask the foreman for trial results before agreeing to changed crew numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about colleagues and later crew cuts, but the work in my cab looks sound today. I will judge a machine after it works a whole shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a full shift reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A truck can arrive late and leave three others waiting across the turn. I would mark the delay and the blocked space, not just say the screen was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the dispatch screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch the dispatcher demonstrate it if the mine uses it, then keep checking against the yard. I am slow with new screens, and a paper queue still gives me a way to check.

say: I separate **2028 dispatch** change from capable wheel-loader robots around 2031.
I want **human shift numbers** before the mine promises an easy change.
think: I could lose **loading hours** at 63 before planned retirement.
I have **three months** saved and some local options, but no confirmed pension income.
do: **Request** written trial dates and a pension estimate now.
**Save** extra shift pay after 2028 if extra shifts are paid.
**Apply** to a nearby mine if loading hours begin falling.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours, with some savings and local options.
S2.quote: A safe machine does not pay my household bills.
fieldNote: **Age 63** at robot arrival is early enough that she may still need full wages.
**Three months** saved softens a short gap but does not establish a retirement income.
**Local job move** depends on falling hours and a written notice.

steps.text: Keep taking paid wheel-loader shifts after 2028
Save extra shift pay if additional shifts are paid
Apply to a nearby mine if loading hours begin falling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI changes dispatch by 2028, while capable wheel-loader robots arrive around 2031. The mine must say how many human loading shifts will remain before it calls the change easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the robots arrive. If the loaders can run a full yard without us, my hours could shrink before I planned to retire. Three months saved gives us some time, and there are a few other mines to ask, but I do not know what the pension will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would request written loader trial dates and a pension estimate. In the first year after 2028 I would keep the shifts offered, put any extra shift pay into savings, and apply to another nearby mine if my hours start falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours, although I am not out of options. I need a real roster, not reassurance from a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which nearby mine would you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the east mine about wheel-loader shifts and ask for a written job notice. I would not leave my current work for a verbal possibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robot is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept the test result and still ask what happens to the people whose shifts disappear. A safe machine does not pay my household bills.

say: I see **2031 dispatch** change before wheel-loader robots around 2034.
I want **proper trials** and real pension figures before reducing hours.
think: I may choose **shorter hours** at 66 if pension income covers costs.
I will not spend **three months** of savings just to retire on a date.
do: **Keep** the loader certificate current this year.
**Attend** a full-shift robot trial after 2031 if held.
**Reduce** shifts only if pension income and savings cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, with time to see a tested result.
S3.quote: I would not buy a certificate from our savings just in case.
fieldNote: **Age 66** at capable robots is a possible retirement point, conditional on monthly income.
**Trial observation** focuses on a stopped loader and how the yard stays safe.
**Paid instruction** remains only a possibility tied to proven equipment and remaining work.

steps.text: Keep the wheel-loader certificate current while working
Wait to reduce shifts until pension and savings cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2031 changes the dispatch desk, with capable wheel-loader robots around 2034. A few years more means the mine can trial equipment properly and workers can check their pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. I might be able to choose shorter hours then, but only if the pension covers our monthly costs. I do not want to spend three months of savings just to claim I retired on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the pension statement with my partner this year and keep the loader certificate current. In the first year after 2031 I would visit a full-shift robot trial if the mine holds one, then reduce my own shifts only if pension income and savings cover ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not hurried. I can work with a tested result and real pension figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch at the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the truck queue when one loader stops for maintenance. The yard still needs a safe path while people repair a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a control course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the mine offers paid instruction on proven equipment and a real loading job remains. I would not buy a certificate from our savings just in case.

say: I separate **2036 dispatch** change from wheel-loader robots around 2039.
I want **clear work plans** and time for households to check retirement sums.
think: I hope to leave **full shifts** before robots arrive at 71.
I need **pension figures** before treating three months saved as enough.
do: **Keep** leading safe loading shifts for now.
**Review** pension and savings each spring with my partner.
**Cut** shifts after 2036 only if retirement income covers bills.
feel: **Calm** about near-term work, with pension checks still necessary.
S4.quote: A printed route cannot teach the feel of a crowded turning area.
fieldNote: **Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at robots makes planned retirement plausible but unconfirmed.
**Three-month cushion** and regular pay support a calm near-term outlook.
**Hands-on teaching** stays central to how she sees younger operators learning.

steps.text: Keep leading safe wheel-loader shifts for now
Wait to cut shifts until retirement income covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches dispatch in 2036 and capable wheel-loader robots around 2039. A decade gives managers time to explain which work remains and gives families time to check retirement sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the thinking system arrives and 71 at the robot date. I hope to be off full shifts before 71, but I cannot claim a pension amount I have not checked. Three months saved and current pay give us a base for planning, not a promise of retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading loading shifts and review pension and savings with my partner every spring. In the first year after 2036 I would compare those figures with household bills and cut shifts only if the income covers us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, though I remain careful about the pension. The robot date is far enough away to make a proper plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my new coworker Petra how to place a truck when a loader is stopped. A printed route cannot teach the feel of a crowded turning area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe shifts if the mine offers them and ask at another nearby mine. I would rather work another season than leave my partner with unpaid bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable wheel-loader robots around 2031 could cut my hours while I still expect to work. Written trial dates and human shift numbers would help us plan. I also need an honest pension estimate before deciding whether fewer shifts are affordable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when a truck line blocks the turn. A loading plan drawn on a screen still needs somebody who has watched a crowded yard.

headlineQuote: A loading plan drawn on a screen still needs somebody who has watched a crowded yard.
portrait: **Olga, 58**, leads wheel-loader shifts and judges truck queues from years of work in a crowded mine yard.
**Typical pay** and three months saved support the household now, while pension income remains unconfirmed.
**Familiar checks** guide her; she never uses AI and wants full-shift proof before changing the crew.
**Fast AGI** makes her anxious because 2028 dispatch change precedes possible loading cuts around 2031.
**Longer warning** lets her test retirement figures and teach trainees while keeping paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves the shortest time before capable wheel-loader robots may cut her hours at 63.
whatWouldHelp: **Written trial dates** and human shift numbers would show whether her work is at risk.
**A pension estimate** would help her decide if fewer shifts can cover household bills.
